extraction.name: SeamlessAlign
extraction.description: SeamlessAlign is a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations created to support multilingual and multimodal machine translation. The paper describes it as the largest open dataset for multimodal translation to date, totaling 470,000 hours and covering 37 languages, with speech-to-text and speech-to-speech alignments mined from large-scale raw audio and text corpora.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The paper describes creating SeamlessAlign by starting with a large collection of raw audio from a publicly available repository of crawled web data, chunking files into overlapping segments, applying speech language identification, using sentence-segmented text data drawn from NLLB on the text side, and then mining speech-text and speech-speech translation pairs in a shared embedding space. It also states that the work used 1 million hours of open speech audio data for self-supervised speech pre-training.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping; Software Collection; Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: We note that some samples from the evaluation data were missing (in 8 out of 21 languages: Catalan, German, Estonian, French, Italian, Mongolian, Persian, and Portuguese).
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data included 4 million hours of raw audio originating from a publicly available repository of crawled web data, approximately 1 million hours of which were in English, and sentence-segmented text data drawn from NLLB. The paper also states that 1 million hours of open speech audio data were used for self-supervised speech representation learning.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: During annotation, 3 annotators examined each source-target audio pair (or audio-text pair) and evaluated the item for semantic similarity using the XSTS protocol; prior to annotating, all annotators went through a set of monolingual English practice evaluations with score justifications; in cases where the 3 annotators had a disagreement of score values of 2 or more, 2 additional annotators evaluated the same item again; for MOS, annotators rated clarity of speech, sound quality, and naturalness on a 1-5 Likert scale.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The median score over annotators of the same audio pair was taken for each evaluation sentence pair; for overall direction scores, the mean of this median score was reported across all evaluated items; language-level scores were calibrated using the mean score on the calibration set for the crew of annotators evaluating a given language direction.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Amazon Mechanical Turk; Whisper-Medium; Whisper-Large-v2; ETOX
extraction.rai:dataBiases: SeamlessM4T overgeneralizes to masculine forms when translating from neutral terms (with an average preference of ∼10%) while showing a lack of robustness when varying gender by an amount of ∼3%; masculine representation is predominant in most of the datasets analyzed; Zulu is very often confused with Nyanja, Igbo with Yoruba, and Modern Standard Arabic with Moroccan Arabic and Egyptian Arabic in the speech LID model
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Scaling to all 100 languages in SeamlessAlign was not done and mining was focused on 37 target languages; some source languages are evaluated zero-shot due to lack of supervision; the current version is not intended for long-form translation and was trained on short text and speech inputs, so translating longer sequences might result in quality degradation; the model is trained on general domain data and is not intended for domain specific inputs such as medical or legal domain; translations cannot be used as certified translations; Fleurs test sets differ slightly across language pairs and human evaluation used limited speaker diversity and typically only 3 annotators per sentence; word-list-based toxicity detection over-detects context-dependent terms and depends on precise tokenization, while ASR before lexical matching adds errors that tend to lead to false negatives; noun-list-based gender representation analysis relies on linguistic gender clues as a proxy and uses a limited noun set; S2ST outputs showed truncation and omission issues, especially for longer source audio durations
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors argue SeamlessM4T could augment "world-readiness" by lowering barriers in cross-lingual communication, improving accessibility for people who lack reading or writing skills and for people who are blind or visually impaired, and helping with languages that have multiple writing systems; they also warn that some users may experience more difficulties than others because performance may vary by gender, race, accent, or language, and that S2ST may carry higher interactional risks around mistranslations or toxicity in live conversations; they state SeamlessM4T-fueled applications should be viewed as an augmentation device rather than a replacement for language learning or reliable human interpreters, especially in high-stakes legal or medical decision-making
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The authors note that the training data were mined from publicly available web sources and that although they invested heavily in data cleaning, personally identifiable information may not be entirely eliminated
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: research in speech and text translation; automatic speech recognition; speech-to-speech translation; speech-to-text translation; text-to-speech translation; text-to-text translation; text-to-speech synthesis
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: We use the top 400 hours of SeamlessAlign in each of 33 X–eng directions and the top 200 hours in each of 29 eng–X directions based on Sonar alignment scores. We added up to 2,500 hours of mined speech-to-speech data from SeamlessAlign per language direction depending on its availability. To address this shortage of labeled data, we resort to pseudo-labeling the ASR data with a multilingual T2TT model. To overcome this data scarcity, it is common practice to use TTS models to convert text from speech-to-text datasets into synthetic speech. To overcome these challenges, we circumvented the need for synthesizing speech and trained multilingual text-to-unit (T2U) models on all the 36 target speech languages. These models can directly convert the text into target discrete units and can be trained on ASR datasets that are readily available.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: On the text side, we rely entirely on the same dataset deployed in NLLB. The same data sources, cleaning, and filtering steps are used and run at scale with our Stopes library. Firstly, we deduplicated the audio file URLs found in the repository, downloaded the audio files, and resampled at 16KHz. Subsequently, we filtered out the non-speech data with a bespoke audio event detection (AED) model. First, we used an open Voice Activity Detection (VAD) model to split audio files into shorter segments. We removed special tokens such as <silence> and <no-speech> from the verbatim transcriptions. We additionally perform length filtering to remove examples exceeding a maximum text length of 100 sub-word tokens and pairs with a skewed text-to-audio length ratio that exceeds 5 sub-words per second. Following NLLB Team et al. [2022], we implemented a toxicity filter. This removes pairs that have toxicity imbalance. In addition, we also applied a length filter. We removed pairs in which the utterance is shorter than 0.1 seconds or longer than 50 seconds. We also removed pairs in which the text is longer than 250 sub-words. Lastly, we removed pairs in which the text contains more than 20% of emojis, more than 50% of punctuations, or more than 50% of spaces. To remove outlier samples from our paired data, we filtered based on the number of seconds of audio generated per text token length ratio, discarding any pair with a ratio exceeding 0.5.
